paragraphs.text: BISHOP FAUSTUS, ON THE RATIONALE OF THE FAITH.
I.
What answer should be given to those who read in the Gospel, "The Father is greater than I," and understand it in such a way that they blasphemously claim the Son is lesser in his divinity?
Answer.

On the authority of all the Scriptures, there are two births in Christ. One is from the Father and knows no beginning, for we read: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God"; and he who was in the beginning encloses every beginning within himself. From his mother, however, he took a beginning, as we read through Isaiah: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel," which is interpreted "God with us": that is, majesty hidden in human frailty. So too we read in John the Evangelist: "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." "In us" means in the frailty of our body.

Likewise, concerning the virgin Mary's giving birth: "And the gate was shut and was not opened." And as if someone had asked why it was not opened, he added: "because the Lord passed through it." The shut gate is the seal of chastity, the integrity of undefiled flesh. For she whom the conception had rather sanctified was not violated by the birth.

Likewise, concerning the twofold substance of God and man in Christ: "And they shall be," it says, "two in one flesh," that is, God and man, one Christ. The Apostle taught that this should be understood of Christ and the Church, that is, of Christ's body, for he says: "And they shall be two in one flesh. But I speak of Christ and the Church." He set this out openly to the Romans: "Our fathers, from whom is Christ according to the flesh." Having affirmed the flesh of the man, he then affirms what belongs to God, saying: "who is God over all, blessed for ever." Here the Son's preeminence is declared so complete that nothing greater could be said of the Father. For if he had a beginning, he would not be over all things but among all things, which by their condition as things made are contained within a beginning. But Christ, because he is equal to the Father, is bound by no law of time or of age. To the Philippians, too, the Apostle plainly proclaims the two births and two substances of Christ, saying: "Who, though he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant." The volumes of the New and Old Testaments are full of such rules. Likewise Job, that outstanding prophet, proclaims: "And in my flesh I shall see God." He prophesied this of the time when the deity of Christ was clothed in the garment of our flesh.

Since, then, as we said before, the Word became flesh, and it is established that man and God are two in one flesh, he speaks to the Father now as man, now as God; now as the visible one born of his mother, now as the invisible one born of the Father. Hear the words of the man. He himself says in the Gospel: "The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." Now let this poor Son of Man show his riches in the glory of his divinity: "All things," he says, "that the Father has are mine." In saying "all things" he left nothing here that he would have less than the Father. "All things" means the power, the substance and the majesty of the one deity. Who would not tremble to call him lesser, who as a truthful witness makes himself equal to the Father universally and in all respects? As the Evangelist declares of him: "This is why the Jews sought [?] to kill him, because he called God his Father, making himself equal to God." And to the Philippians: "He did not think it robbery to be equal to God." That is, the equality of divinity which the rebel angel tried to seize by robbery, Christ possesses by nature.

So when you believe him as he says, in the substance of a man, that he is lesser, believe him also when he declares himself equal in the substance of divinity. Let the Son of Man speak: "The Father," he says, "is greater than I." Let the Son of God speak: "I and the Father are one." As man he hungers; as God he fills five thousand hungry people with five loaves, his creation serving him. As man he hangs on the cross; as God he brings the thief from the cross into paradise, as these deeds are proclaimed throughout the whole world, saying: "Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." At that time the Lord's body was in the tomb, his soul in the underworld, and his divinity in paradise and in heaven and everywhere, embracing all things within itself in the surpassing immensity of its majesty.

As man he is called lesser when he is seized, scourged, crucified, dies and is buried; as God he is raised up into heaven by the power of the resurrection. As man he underwent death; as God he is above death. By this rule he is now poor, now rich; now lesser, now equal; now Lord, now servant.

Let him be believed lesser than the Father, then, when the creator of the angels is made a little lower than the angels, as we read in the eighth Psalm: "You made him a little lower than the angels." Let him be called lesser than the Father, then, when he is written to have taken the form of a servant, when he is found to be even younger than his mother, when he says of himself in the twenty-first Psalm: "They pierced my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones." That he is called lesser than the Father according to the flesh and according to the man is made clear by countless testimonies of Scripture.

Of his divinity the Apostle speaks thus to Titus: "The grace of God our Saviour has appeared," and again: "looking for the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ." It is a monstrous sacrilege that through the unbelieving blasphemies of men he should be called lesser whom Truth itself declares to be the great God. For the apostle Thomas too, in the Gospel of John, recognized after the resurrection the body of the crucified man by the marks of the nails, and with apostolic and evangelical authority confessed the God who lay hidden within the man, saying: "My Lord and my God." If faith is present, the reason is plain why the sacred volumes declare Christ now lesser than the Father and now equal to him. As he himself says of himself: "I am the first and the last." Recognize without doubt that he who is first cannot have anyone before him. Again: "I am the Alpha and the Omega." Just as no letter comes before A, so it is certain that the Son of God is second to none, because he is God.
II.
What shall we answer those who say that the Holy Spirit is a lesser God, or, what is more wicked, declare with headlong impiety that he is a minister rather than God?
Answer.

How can he be called a creature who is shown to be the creator of the Lord from Mary? For we read: "conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary." Christ was conceived not from the substance of the Holy Spirit but by his power, not by generation but by his command and blessing. And as he was appointed by the Father, so too was he appointed by the Holy Spirit to redeem our wickedness, as he himself says of himself through Isaiah: "The Father and his Spirit have sent me."

If the Holy Spirit is believed to be lesser, how does the Son testify that he was sent by the Holy Spirit just as by the Father? The Holy Spirit himself spoke in the apostles; he himself burned in the prophets, as the blessed apostle Peter says in his epistle: "Prophecy was not brought by men, but holy men of God spoke inspired by the Holy Spirit." And the Saviour speaks thus to his disciples in Matthew: "It is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit." Likewise David, full of the Holy Spirit, declares in a clear voice who was speaking through him, saying: "I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me." So when the vessels of God, drunk with the Holy Spirit, speak and say, "Thus says the Lord God," or, "The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken," it is plain that this Lord God is the Holy Spirit.

And to the Corinthians the Apostle shows clearly that the Holy Spirit is God when he says: "You are the temple of God." And he went on to teach who this God is, saying: "The Holy Spirit dwells in you." So the God of the temple and the Holy Spirit who dwells in the temple are one person. And in the Acts of the Apostles Peter speaks clearly of the deity of the Holy Spirit, saying to Ananias: "Who drove you to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to men," he says, "but to God." What could be plainer? He is said to have made his vow to God, and he is convicted of lying to the Holy Spirit. If the Holy Spirit were not God, the injury of this sacrilegious falsehood would never have reached him. Again the Apostle's voice says to the Corinthians: "Do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit? Glorify and carry God in your body." They are surely commanded to carry the God whose temples they are said to be.
III.
What shall we answer those who say: "The Father cannot fail to be prior, since he is named first in baptism"?
Answer.
The Holy Spirit too is first, for without him it is not enough to have named the first. But he who is one and alone in the substance of the three admits neither number nor order.
IV.
What shall we answer those who blaspheme with impious mouth, saying: "The Holy Spirit is not God, because he has done nothing as God"?
Answer.

Let us see whether nothing divine appears in his works. In the first place, remission of sins is not granted unless the Holy Spirit is invoked. And since sins are not forgiven without the Holy Spirit, let us recognize that this too was said most plainly of him: "No one can forgive sins but God alone." So do not doubt that the one you see restoring man is the author of man.

He who at the first made man without sin is the same who at the second, as regenerator together with the Father and the Son, frees man from the chain of sin. See how the Apostle, in the epistle to the Corinthians, celebrates the works and powers of the Holy Spirit, saying: "To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another the gift of healings in the one Spirit, to another kinds of tongues, the working of miracles, to another prophecy. All these are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills."

And how can we say that he is a minister, who has performed the miracles of such great gifts by the decision of his own will and by right of lordship? Of him we read through the prophet, where the Trinity is distinguished: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power." The prophet said "the Spirit of his mouth," not "of his work," so that you would know he proceeded from the very substance of the Father. And so it says: "the Spirit who proceeds from the Father." "By the Spirit of his mouth all their power": the powers of the heavens, that is, the angels, dominions, thrones and principalities. Truth declares that these were created through the Holy Spirit just as through the Father and the Son.

So you cannot call him a creature without monstrous sacrilege, when you see that he is the creator of the whole heavenly host. Accordingly, in the distinct properties and number of the three persons, acknowledge one power, one glory, one nature. Otherwise, by denying the three persons, you will deny the Son or the Holy Spirit along with the Jews and the Patripassians; or, by denying the one substance, you will be shown to believe in three gods along with the pagans.
